Judgment

1 By this judgment I will dispose of appeal u/sec.374 Cr.PC. filed on behalf of convict Dinesh Kumar against the judgment dated 15.02.2014 and order on sentence dated 21.02.2014 passed by Sh.
Gaurav Rao, Ld. ACMM-II, Patiala House Court, New Delhi.
2 The brief facts of the case as per record and from trial court record are that accused is running an establishment namely M/s Gupta Store, Shop no. 3, R. K. Puram, Kali Badi Marg, New Delhi.
On 21.01.2002 at about 4.00 p.m. Food Inspector Sh. Jeet Ram visited the said place and purchased 750 grams of "Dal Arhar" from accused.
FI was accompanied with SDM/LHA Sh. S. M. Haider.
The said Arhar Dal was purchased for the purposes of analysis under PFA Act.
The same sample was divided into three parts, packed as per Rules of PFA.
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.
As per the report of Analyst, sample did not confirm to the standard because "The sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter viz. Tartrazine."
During investigation, accused Dinesh sent a letter to FI stating that he purchased the Dal from M/s Vijay Trading Company run by Sh. Vijay Aggarwal.

Matter was investigated and it was found that the accused Dinesh purchased the Dal from Vijay Aggarwal, so both were made accused, in the trial court.

1 3
As the sample was failed, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 17.12.2003 with the court.
Accused was summoned.
He has exercised his right u/sec.13(2) PFA Act to get the sample analyzed by CFL.

CFL reported "I am of the opinion that the sample bearing no.
SMH/LHA/3670 does not conform to standards of split pulse (Dal) Arhar as per PFA Rules, 1955 (Synthetic colour Tartrazine detected)."
4

Charge was framed against accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) (b)
(j) (m) read with sec.7 of PFA Act, 1954 punishable u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act.
5

After trial, vide judgment dated 15.02.2014 accused Dinesh Kumar was convicted for offence u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act and vide order on sentence dated 21.02.2014, accused was directed to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 18 months and fine of Rs.5,000/- and in default of payment of fine SI of 30 days.
However, accused Vijay Aggarwal was acquitted.

6 In this appeal, the accused has assailed the judgment on the following grounds:-
(i) Non-compliance of Rule 14 of PFA Rules i.e. the bottles, jhaba etc., were not made clean and dried at the spot by the food inspector or any other official.
(ii) Appellant is protected in view of Sec.19(2) PFA as he had established that he purchased the sample commodity from some other person and sold the same in the same condition.
(iii) Benefit be given to the appellant under Food & Safety Standards Act (hereinafter called FSSA).
7 No reply was filed by respondent/state and the matter was argued orally.
8 I have gone through the record, Trial Court record and have heard the submissions of Ld. counsel for appellant and Ld. SPP for State.
9 It is argued that compliance u/sec.14 PFA Rules was not proved on record by the prosecution.
It is stated that witnesses are deposing differently with respect to the cleanliness of jhaba etc.
It is further stated that it was the duty of the prosecution to prove these facts.
These arguments were also addressed before the trial court.
The relevant part of the judgment dealing with these arguments are from para 30 to 46 of the judgment.
From the perusal of the record, it appears that prosecution was able to state that the bottles, jhaba etc., used for sampling the commodity, was clean.
There is no other fact on record.
So, in these circumstances, the prosecution was able to prove that compliance u/sec.14 of PFA Act was properly done and the relevant portion of the judgment is thus upheld.

2 10
It is further argued that accused had purchased the sample commodity from Vijay Trading Company, At I-7, Shardhananad Market vide kacha bill Mark Y.

It is stated that on account of Sec.19(2) PFA Act, accused is protected against prosecution as it has established that the commodity was purchased from some other person and sold in the same condition.

This leg of arguments were dealt by the court from para 23 to 29.
11
On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. APP for State that the no evidence was led to establish/prove the said kacha bill and hence the same cannot be read in evidence.

It is further stated that due to that reason, there is no evidence on record that the lot from which the sample was taken, was purchased by accused from M/s Vijay Trading Company, At I-7, Shardhananad Market.
12 As far as this argument is concerned, the bill Ex.PW- D/A (photocopy Mark Y) was sent to the prosecution/FI by the accused vide Ex.PW1/K.
So, this particular document is part of the documents relied by the prosecution.
Considering this document as that of opposite party, the accused can rely on this document even without proving it.

Moreover, in the testimony of PW1 i.e. cross-examination dated 27.05.2009, he had stated "I was satisfied that vendor purchased the sample commodity from M/s Vijay Trading Company through this kacha bill (Mark Y).
So, due to this admission, the document get proved.
So, accordingly, prosecution itself admitted that the accused purchased the sample commodity from M/s Vijay Trading Company.
13 It is argued that the sample commodity was taken from an open gunny bag and was not stored in its original condition and thus benefit u/sec.19(2) PFA Act cannot be extended to accused.

14 As far as Sec.19(2) PFA Act is concerned, the same is as follows:-
"19(2)-A Vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded articles of food if he proves:-
(a) that he purchased the article of food- (i) in a case where a license is prescribed for the sale thereof, from a duly licensed manufacturer, distributor or dealer,
(ii) in any other case, from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer, with a written warranty in the prescribed form; and (iii) that the article of food while in his possession was properly stored and that he sold it in the same state as he purchased it."
So, Sec. 19(2) PFA Act is exception to the general rule.
However the onus is upon the accused to make out its case in Sec.19(2) PFA Act.

So, he has to prove that he has bought the sample commodity from a supplier and second the said commodity was stored in the same condition as that Dinesh Kumar vs The State (Da) on 16 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65123011/
3 bought from the supplier.

15 Now whether the mere opening of the stitched sack/container and taking out the commodity alters its condition and takes the case out of the purview of Sec.19(2) of PFA Act, is dealt by Superior Courts.
16 In A. P. Grain and Sweets Merchant Association Vs. Union of India, WP NO. 468/69, DOD 31.03.1970 in para 13, it is laid down:-

entities.text: A. P. Grain and Sweets Merchant Association Vs. Union of India, WP NO. 468/69
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "The argument of counsel for petitioners that the provision that a retail seller who opens a container of a branded article of food loses even the limited protection under section 19(2) is without substance.

Clause (b) of subj-section (2) of section 19 does not prove nor does it imply, that if the container of a branded article is opened, the article of food ceases to be in the same state in which the vendor purchased it.

If the article of foods is sold in the same condition in which it was purchased from a licensed manufacturer or dealer, or was purchased with a warranty, the vendor will not lose the protection of sub-section (2) of section 19 merely because he opened the container.

If the vendor has obtained the article from a licensed manufacture,
distributor or from a manufacture, distributor or dealer, he is protected, provided he has properly stored the article and sells it in the same state as he purchased the article, even if it turns out that the article was adulterated or misbranded."
So, accordingly, the retailer can sell the article by opening the container/bag but with condition that he should have stored the article in the same condition as it was purchased from supplier.
17 Moreover, the status of vendor and supplier is further clarified in the law laid down by Superior Courts.

"In Aboo Vs. FI, 2003 (1) FAC 81 and FI Vs. M. H. Shoukathali, 1989 (1) FAC 261,
Hon. High Court of Kerala had stated "But the question whether by opening its package the "state" of the food article would be disturbed or changed.

entities.text: FI Vs. M. H. Shoukathali, 1989 (1) FAC 261
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: is primarily intended to give protection to the retail dealers.
If a retailer is not permitted to sell the article in retail after he purchases it from a wholesale dealer it would affect the trading system of retail business.
One of the usual modes of retail business is to buy articles in bulk and sell them in smaller quantities.

The Legislature would never have intended that the retailer would be permitted to avail the defence envisaged in S.19(2) only if he sells the food article in the same package or container without opening them.
There cannot be a hard and fast rule that every article is liable to change its state when it is disinterred from its container.
Coriander is certainly not that type of article which undergoes transformation through disinterment from its package.

No cereals or other edible grains would lose its state, in normal conditions,
by its exposure from the packages."

4 18
There is no argument/evidence on record which suggests that accused had not sold the commodity in the same condition.
In cross-examination of PW dated 01.02.2011, he has deposed "it is correct that accused no. 1 is not the manufacturer of the sample commodity.
It is correct that the vendor had not applied the colour as detected by the PA and Director CFL in the sample commodity."
So, as per this witness accused has not done any act of adulteration, if any, on his part.
So, in these circumstances, accused is able to prove that he has purchased the commodity/sample commodity from the supplier.
He sold the commodity in the same condition as when bought from the supplier and has not done any adulteration.
19 So, in these circumstances, accused is able to prove that he is exempted by the provisions of warranty as mentioned in Sec.19(2) PFA Act.
20 So, the judgment and order on sentence of the trial court against this accused Dinesh Kumar is set aside.
21 Accused Dinesh Kumar is acquitted of the charges u/sec.16(1A) read with sec.7 of PFA Act.
22 Bail Bond u/sec.437A Cr.P.C. already furnished and accepted for six months.
23 TCR be sent back with copy of the order.
24 File of appeal be consigned to Record Room.
ANNOUNCED
